messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mr. Nguyen is a 51-year-old South Eastern Asian man who works as a policy analyst and has been married for over two decades. His life changed drastically after he experienced a severe natural disaster—a powerful tornado—that tore through his community last year. During the tornado, Mr. Nguyen found himself trapped in a building with broken windows and debris swirling around him. The smell of burning wood and smoke was overwhelming as fires broke out nearby. He felt physically ill from the fear and helplessness, and the unpredictability of the situation only heightened his anxiety. Since then, any feeling of being unwell or exposure to unpredictable situations triggers intense distress and flashbacks for Mr. Nguyen. Mr. Nguyen has come to believe that he can't rely on himself in such situations anymore. His experience during the tornado made him feel utterly vulnerable, and now he is certain that if something goes wrong again, he won’t be able to protect himself or his family. This belief exacerbates his fear of going crazy. He constantly worries about how his heightened reactions might indicate a deeper mental health issue. The thought of losing control in an unpredictable situation terrifies him. This constant vigilance has taken a toll on Mr. Nguyen’s daily life and work. At the office, he avoids attending meetings that might run late or involve unexpected turns, as any unpredictability makes him feel physically ill. Recently, his fear of being unwell led to a significant decrease in productivity, as he would leave early if even a slight feeling of nausea arose. His colleagues have noticed changes in his behavior, but Mr. Nguyen is too afraid to address it directly. At home, the smell of smoke during a cooking mishap can send him into a panic. He has become hypervigilant about any potential fire hazards and insists on checking all appliances repeatedly, which strains his relationship with his wife. She notices that he seems on edge most of the time but is unsure how to help. The unpredictability of everyday life now feels unbearable for Mr. Nguyen. Even small changes in routine can trigger a cascade of anxiety and fear. He had come to believe that these reactions mean he’s going crazy, which further intensifies his negative appraisals about himself. This vicious cycle has led him to become increasingly isolated, both at work and at home. What finally prompted Mr. Nguyen to seek help was an incident where he left a crucial meeting early due to feeling ill. His supervisor noticed the pattern of absenteeism and suggested professional support. Now, as he considers therapy, what frightens him most is the prospect that his fears might indeed be justified—that he won’t be able to function normally again without significant intervention. On the other hand, he hopes that understanding these reactions will provide some relief from the overwhelming anxiety that has come to dominate his life. Mr. Nguyen’s journey since the tornado illustrates a profound shift in how he perceives himself and the world around him. The traumatic event has left deep marks on his psyche, making even minor triggers potent reminders of his vulnerability. His fear of unpredictability and physical illness now fuel each other in a self-reinforcing cycle that he hopes to break through therapy.
